after: ## Robust and secure: what the words mean
alt: A robust program keeps working sensibly with unexpected input and is supported by validation; a secure program only lets authorised users in and is supported by authentication; testing checks both. Validation only checks that data is reasonable: an age of 15 passes a range check of 11 to 18 even if the user is really 16.
caption: Validation makes a program robust, authentication makes it secure, and testing checks both.

alt: Pseudocode and a flowchart for validating an age from 11 to 18. After the first input, while age < 11 OR age > 18 is True the program shows an error message and asks again; once it is False the valid age is used. The REPEAT version instead repeats until age ≥ 11 AND age ≤ 18.
caption: Keep asking until the input passes; the invalid test uses OR, the valid test uses AND.

alt: Three checks, each written as the condition that makes input invalid: presence, LEN(name) = 0; minimum length, LEN(username) < 6; range, qty < 1 OR qty > 20. On a length line from 0 to 7, lengths 0 to 5 fail the minimum-length check and 6 or more pass; the empty string, length 0, is already rejected, so a separate presence check is not needed.
caption: Checks can overlap: the minimum-length check already rejects an empty string.

alt: A flowchart of the login routine. The username and password are input and checked together with AND. If both match, success is set to True; otherwise attempts goes up by 1 and a message says "Incorrect username or password". The loop repeats until success OR attempts = MaxAttempts, then outputs Welcome or access denied.
caption: Check both items with AND; stop on success OR when the attempts run out.

alt: A number line with the valid range 1 to 20 shaded. Normal data 7 is accepted. Boundary values 1 and 20 are accepted, and 0 and 21 just outside are rejected. Erroneous data such as 35, −4 and the text "ten" is rejected. Each type is listed with what the test proves.
caption: Test inside, on and just beyond each limit, plus wrong data, and state the expected result for each.

after: ## Worked example: a test plan for a password rule
alt: Four tests for a rule that passwords must be at least 8 characters. Sunbird42x (10 characters) is normal and accepted; Sunbird4 (8) is boundary and accepted, checking ≥ not >; Sunbird (7) is boundary and rejected as the longest invalid length; the empty string is erroneous and rejected.
caption: Test just on and just below the minimum length, plus a typical and an empty value.
